name: Printing Digits of an Integer from Right to Left
description: Construct a program that prints the digits of an integer from right to left.
code:
#Step 1: Assign initial values to the variables which we need for this program
num = 1234
#Step 2: Print the digits of the integer from right to left
while num > 0 :
    #Step 2.1: Get the last digit in the integer
    last_digit = num % 10
    #Step 2.2: Print the extracted digit
    print(last_digit)
    #Step 2.3: Remove the last digit from the integer
    num = num // 10

commentList: You give the variable num the starting value 1234 so the rest of the code has a concrete integer to work on; this is the number whose digits you will print from right to left.
You use the assignment operator = to store the integer literal 1234 in the name num. In Python this means num now refers to the integer 1234 and you can use numeric operations like % and // on it.

Be careful not to confuse = (assignment) with == (comparison). Also if num is a string (e.g., '1234') or a non-integer, using % and // later will cause errors; negative values or zero change behavior (while num > 0 will skip for num <= 0), so think about those cases.

As a best practice, avoid hard-coding 'magic' numbers in real programs—use a descriptive name (num is fine here), or get the value from the user with num = int(input(...)). Consider handling num == 0 and negative numbers (for example using num = abs(num)) so your program works for more inputs.

commentList: Purpose: This line starts the loop that repeats the digit-extraction steps until there are no more digits left. You use it to process each digit from right to left by running the indented block as long as the condition is true.

Syntax and structure: 'while' is the loop keyword, 'num > 0' is the boolean condition checked before every iteration, and the trailing ':' marks the loop header. You must put the code that runs inside the loop on the next lines and indent them consistently.

Semantics and termination: The condition 'num > 0' means the loop runs only while num is positive. You rely on the code inside the loop (num = num // 10) to decrease num so the loop eventually ends when num becomes 0.

Potential errors and misconceptions: If you forget the ':' or use incorrect indentation, Python raises a SyntaxError. If num is negative the loop will never run, so you might mistakenly skip digits for negative inputs unless you handle the sign (for example with abs(num)).

Common alternative and clarity: Although 'while num:' would also loop for any nonzero value, using 'while num > 0' makes your intent explicit (process positive digits). Be aware that integers do not preserve leading zeros, so you won't print any leading zeros from the original representation.

Best practices: Make sure num is an integer and non-negative before this loop (or convert with abs(num) if you want to handle negatives). Always include a statement inside the loop that reduces num (like integer division) to avoid an infinite loop. If you want to print '0' for input 0, handle that case before the loop because this condition skips looping when num == 0.

commentList: You use this line to extract the last decimal digit of num so you can print the number from right to left; the result is stored in the variable last_digit for the next step.

You are assigning the value of the expression num % 10 to last_digit. The % operator gives the remainder after dividing num by 10, and for positive integers that remainder is exactly the final digit (for example, 1234 % 10 == 4).

Be careful: if num can be negative, the remainder may not match what you expect for a 'digit' (so you should use abs(num) or handle the sign separately). Also avoid using / (true division) here — that would produce a float, not the remainder digit; ensure num is an integer before using %.

As a best practice, consider working on a copy of the original number (for example n = num) if you need to keep num unchanged, and always extract the last digit before you remove it with integer division (num = num // 10) so you don't lose data.

commentList: Purpose: this line sends the extracted digit (last_digit) to the program output so you see each digit as the loop processes the number from right to left.

Syntax and semantics: print(last_digit) is a function call (Python 3) that converts last_digit to text and writes it to standard output. By default it adds a newline after each call, so each digit appears on its own line.

Possible errors and misconceptions: if last_digit were not defined before this line you'd get a NameError; if you run code under Python 2 without from __future__ import print_function you might expect different behavior because print was a statement there. Also remember that if num is 0 the while loop never runs, so you need a separate case if you want to print 0.

Best practices: if you want the digits on one line separated by spaces use print(last_digit, end=' ') or collect digits in a list and join them later. If you need to handle negative numbers, take abs(num) before the loop. Keep in mind print only displays values—it does not modify variables, so any further processing must use the stored values.

commentList: Purpose: This line removes the last digit from num so the while loop can move on to the next digit and eventually stop. Without updating num you would get an infinite loop.

Syntax and semantics: num = num // 10 uses the floor-division operator // to divide num by 10 and assign the integer result back to num. For positive integers this effectively drops the last decimal digit (e.g., 1234 // 10 -> 123).
Why not use / : If you used num = num / 10 you would get a float (e.g., 1234 / 10 -> 123.4). That breaks the digit-extraction logic and can stop the loop from behaving as expected.

Common misconception / pitfalls: For negative numbers // does floor division (rounds down), not simple truncation toward zero (e.g., -1 // 10 -> -1). If you expect to handle negative inputs, take abs(num) first or handle the sign separately.

Best practices: Ensure num is an int before the loop (cast if it comes from user input). If you want shorter code, you can write num //= 10. If you need to keep the original number, work on a copy (e.g., temp = num).

Loop termination note: Each execution of this line reduces num; when num becomes 0 the while condition (num > 0) becomes false and the loop ends, which is why this line is essential to reach the program’s final result.

distractors.description: You might pick this because you think the loop should run while there is more than one digit to process, so stopping at 1 seems reasonable. However, this misses the case when the number reduces to a single digit greater than 0 (for example 1). Step-by-step: with num = 1234 the loop will extract and print 4, 3, and 2, but when num becomes 1 the condition num > 1 is false and the loop stops — the final digit 1 is never printed. In other words, this condition drops the last single-digit case and yields incomplete output. The mistake is an off-by-one termination check: the loop must allow the final single-digit extraction, but this version prevents that, so the program fails to print the last digit.

You might choose this because you want to allow the loop to run when num is zero 'just in case' — it seems safe to include equality. But that creates a serious problem: once num becomes 0, printing last_digit will print 0 and then integer division of 0 by 10 yields 0 again, so num stays 0 forever and the loop never terminates. Step-by-step: starting from 1234 the loop will print digits until num becomes 0; then it will repeatedly print 0 and never exit. This is an infinite loop caused by allowing the condition to be true when num is already the sentinel value. The key mistake is failing to stop the loop when num reaches the stopping value that signals 'no more digits'; widening the condition to include that value prevents progress and leads to unbounded repetition.

You might pick this because it reads naturally: keep looping until the number becomes zero. For positive starting values this appears to work — the loop extracts digits until num becomes 0. However, this line treats positive and negative numbers the same. If num is negative, repeated integer floor-division by 10 will not necessarily move the value to 0; it can approach and stick at -1 in Python, so the condition stays true and the loop never ends. Step-by-step: with a positive input like 1234 you will get the expected digits, but with negative inputs the loop can become infinite. Using this check also masks the intent of only processing positive digits; it relies on a generic non-zero sentinel rather than a condition that matches the intended domain. In short, this alternative is plausible but unsafe when num may be negative — it can cause an infinite loop — and it fails to enforce the intended positive-only stopping condition.
